A recently released GOP-authored report by the House Benghazi Select Committee has sparked sharp partisan conflict regarding the 2012 attacks in Libya. The investigation concludes that the Obama administration, including former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, failed to provide adequate security in Benghazi and knowingly misled the public regarding the nature of the violence.

The report highlights significant discrepancies between public statements and private communications made by administration officials immediately following the attack. While officials publicly attributed the violence to protests spurred by an anti-Islam video, private emails and phone calls—such as those between Secretary Clinton and the Libyan President as well as her daughter—indicated that they believed the attack was a pre-planned terrorist act by an Al Qaeda-affiliated group. The investigation suggests this narrative was chosen to protect political interests rather than reflect the intelligence available at the time.

Additionally, the report details operational confusion during the crisis, noting that State Department officials on an emergency conference call debated whether Marines should wear uniforms or civilian clothing. While the State Department maintains that this discussion did not delay the military response, critics argue it exemplifies a misguided focus on optics over the immediate rescue of personnel.

Democratic members of the committee, led by Rep. Elijah Cummings, have vehemently criticized the report as a partisan exercise. Cummings described the investigation as one of the "saddest exercises" of his career, accusing Republicans of hiding evidence, locking Democrats out of interviews, and failing to find any new evidence of wrongdoing regarding "stand-down" orders or gun trading. Despite the political friction, the report adds extensive detail to the historical record of the tragedy, though it leaves the interpretation of those facts deeply divided along party lines. A supplemental report by Representatives Jim Jordan and Mike Pompeo further argues that the administration intentionally provided a false story to the American people. The release marks the culmination of a two-year investigation that has cost over $7 million. The findings are likely to play a significant role in the ongoing political discourse surrounding the upcoming presidential election. The report is comprehensive and detailed. The committee has finished its work. The debate continues. The end.

reference_answer: The Republican-led House Benghazi committee released its final report Tuesday after two years of investigations. The 800-page report lays out the committee's findings on the 2012 attacks in Libya that left four Americans dead. Here's what you need to know: Benghazi is "unlikely to be a potent tool for weakening Clinton" in the general election, as the committee and report have little credibility and aren't seen as serious by many, the Los Angeles Times reports. Easily distilling the massive report, the Washington Post lays out its five "most serious accusations," including that the CIA "missed warning signs" and "misread how dangerous Libya ... was at the time." New evidence of “culpability or wrongdoing” on Clinton's part is lacking in the report, despite it being “one of the longest, costliest, and most bitterly partisan congressional investigations in history," according to the New York Times. Given a lack of new evidence against Clinton, the Weekly Standard uses the report as a tool for blaming Obama. “The Obama administration knowingly provided the American people a false story about the Benghazi attack, its causes, and its consequences," the Standard states. How various government agencies responded to the Benghazi crisis is one of the more interesting aspects of the report. According to Politico, a conference call in the midst of the attack included a conversation about whether Marines should wear their uniforms if deployed. Marines changed in and out of their uniforms multiple times while waiting for an answer and were never deployed. According to the Hill, a Democratic lawmaker on the House Benghazi committee calls it "one of the saddest exercises I've ever engaged in" during 20 years in Congress. He accuses Republicans of hiding the final report from Democrats to avoid having it fact-checked. Zeroing in on what it calls the "most revealing paragraph" in the report, Vox concludes there's a pattern of spinning "non-damning facts as damning" for the Obama administration. The paragraph in question admits there were no US forces close enough to prevent the attack but insists that, in itself, was a failure on the part of the White House. "I think it's time to move on," the AP quotes Clinton as saying after the release of the report, which she says includes nothing not previously discovered by an accountability board.
